clue.text: The old woman who lived in a shoe had one, and it's a big deal!

definitions.text: The old woman who lived in a shoe had one
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the nursery-rhyme woman had so many children that her home was packed to capacity
second meaning: in poker a hand of three of a kind plus a pair, a strong deal of the cards

explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme's old woman 'had so many children she didn't know what to do'; 'deal' then switches to card-playing.
explanation.definitionFit: A home crammed with occupants and a strong poker hand share one two-word name.

clue.text: See 30 across
Do toadies show an absence of something important? Yes, possibly at last!

indicators.note: at last means the shuffled letters come at the end of the answer

parts.note: a lack is an absence of something

indicators.note: possibly means the three letters of the word yes may be rearranged

explanation.surface: Do flatterers show they lack something vital? Perhaps they finally say yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' shuffles the reply word into EYS and 'at last' puts it at the end. The question also plays on 'lack keys': toadies lack something important.
explanation.definitionFit: Lackeys are servile followers, the flatterers who fawn on someone powerful.

clue.text: How the captain of the Pinafore swore!

definitions.text: How the captain of the Pinafore swore!

parts.words: How the captain of the Pinafore swore!
parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's HMS Pinafore the captain boasts he never swears, then admits it happens almost never

explanation.walkthrough: The famous exchange runs 'What, never?' 'No, never!' 'What, never?' 'Well, hardly ever!'
explanation.definitionFit: The captain claims to use bad language almost never, which is the stock phrase meaning very rarely.

clue.text: Raises the little pies, just like obnoxious newcomers!

parts.note: ups is a verb meaning raises, as in 'ups the price'
tarts are small pies

explanation.surface: Someone lifts the small pastries, behaving like pushy new arrivals.
explanation.definitionFit: Upstarts are people who have risen suddenly and act with arrogance.

clue.text: The final note to a list he had made short–with acid applied.

parts.words: The final note to a list
parts.note: etc, et cetera, is often written at the end of a list
he had contracts to he'd

explanation.surface: A list-maker shortens his last note, then treats it with acid.
explanation.definitionFit: Etching uses acid to bite a design into a metal plate.

clue.text: They were found upon the Swanee River, when they were old.

definitions.text: They were found upon the Swanee River, when they were old.

parts.words: They were found upon the Swanee River, when they were old.
parts.note: Stephen Foster's song beginning 'Way down upon the Swanee River' names the people at home there, with 'old' in front

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Folks at Home' is the Stephen Foster song whose first line is 'Way down upon the Swanee River'; drop the 'old' the clue has already supplied.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's people by the river are the old folks, so the plain word for people fills the gap.

clue.text: Squashes down where some people live, sent astray.

parts.note: a flat is an apartment

indicators.note: astray means the word sent wanders off into a new letter order

explanation.surface: Someone crushes the place where people live and sends them wandering.
explanation.definitionFit: To flatten something is to press or crush it down level.

clue.text: In Paris the guy who takes care of the horses has plenty of space to sit in.

definitions.text: plenty of space to sit in

parts.note: le is French for the

parts.words: guy who takes care of the horses
parts.note: a groom looks after horses

explanation.surface: A French stable hand enjoys a roomy seat.
explanation.definitionFit: Legroom is room for a seated person's legs, as in an aircraft or car.

clue.text: Harems show the direction an old piece of cloth takes, to possibly soil the result.

parts.note: SE is the compass abbreviation for southeast
a rag is a scrap of old cloth

indicators.note: possibly means the letters of soil might be set in another order

explanation.surface: Harem quarters show which way an old rag drifts, perhaps dirtying things.
explanation.definitionFit: A seraglio is the women's quarters of a Turkish palace, the harem.

clue.text: See 13
The London maid gets grand before the queen–and that's how the knights got around!

definitions.text: that's how the knights got around

indicators.note: the earlier pieces are placed before the queen's letters in the answer

parts.note: a char, short for charwoman, is a British cleaning woman
G is the usual abbreviation for grand, a thousand
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the queen's royal cipher

explanation.surface: A London housemaid marries well before meeting the queen, while knights ride about.
explanation.walkthrough: A char is a British charwoman, a cleaning lady; ER is the royal cipher of Elizabeth Regina. 'before' sets the maid and grand ahead of the queen.
explanation.definitionFit: A charger is a war horse, the mount a medieval knight rode into battle.

clue.text: You would be surprised to meet another driver headed for you here.

definitions.text: You would be surprised to meet another driver headed for you here.

parts.words: You would be surprised to meet another driver headed for you here.
parts.note: on a road where traffic may travel in a single direction, an oncoming car would be a shock

explanation.definitionFit: On a road where traffic is permitted in a single direction, oncoming vehicles should never appear.

clue.text: With a lot of money, as some say, the young fellow could get mixed up with the abridged Oxford English Dictionary.

definitions.text: With a lot of money, as some say

indicators.note: mixed up means the boy and the dictionary letters are jumbled together

parts.note: a lad is a young fellow
OED is the short form of the Oxford English Dictionary

explanation.surface: A rich young man gets tangled up with a shortened dictionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as some say' warns that the definition is slang; 'mixed up' jumbles LAD and OED together.
explanation.definitionFit: Loaded is slang for very rich, having plenty of cash.

clue.text: Someone like Huey entertaining himself at the Victrola with these?

definitions.text: Someone like Huey entertaining himself at the Victrola with these?

parts.words: Someone like Huey entertaining himself at the Victrola with these?
parts.note: A Victrola is an old record player, and the discs played on one at 33 rpm have the answer's name

explanation.surface: A man called Huey amuses himself at the gramophone with some discs.
explanation.walkthrough: Huey Long, the Louisiana governor, supplies the first word; someone at a Victrola (a brand of phonograph) is playing; what he plays are records.
explanation.definitionFit: LPs are vinyl discs holding long recordings, played on a phonograph at slow speed.

clue.text: To describe something like "not feeling good," you and I get to badly treat the rest of it!

parts.note: ill means not feeling well
us is you and I

indicators.note: badly means the letters of treat are mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: Describing feeling unwell, we go on to mistreat everything else.
explanation.definitionFit: To illustrate is to explain or depict something with examples or pictures.

clue.text: Often rounded up by the police, as one imagines.

definitions.text: Often rounded up by the police
definitions.meaning: first meaning: people the police believe may have committed a crime
second meaning: to suspect something is to imagine or believe it is so

explanation.walkthrough: A noun meaning people under suspicion and a verb meaning 'imagines'.
explanation.definitionFit: Persons thought guilty are rounded up by police, and to suspect is also to guess or imagine.

clue.text: Worshiped by some as a favorite, it's not the "holy" type a onetime sportscaster often spouted.

definitions.text: Worshiped by some as a favorite
definitions.note: a noun phrase in sense: something revered beyond criticism

parts.words: it's not the "holy" type a onetime sportscaster often spouted
parts.note: baseball announcers such as Phil Rizzuto made 'Holy cow!' a catchphrase; this cow is sacred, not holy

explanation.surface: A revered favourite, unlike the exclamation a baseball broadcaster used to shout.
explanation.walkthrough: Phil Rizzuto, the Yankees broadcaster, was famous for crying 'Holy cow!'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sacred cow is an idea or institution treated as above criticism, like the venerated animal in Hinduism.

clue.text: A crystalline solid in back–for those who must have gone to school.

definitions.text: those who must have gone to school

parts.note: alum is a crystalline double sulphate salt

indicators.note: back means the little word in is turned round and read the other way

explanation.surface: A salt crystal at the back is somehow for former schoolgoers.
explanation.definitionFit: Graduates or former students of a school or college are its alumni.

clue.text: Sounds like a witticism of Oliver Wendell–but it's really just like house material.

indicators.note: sounds like says the spoken phrase gives the answer when heard, not as written

parts.note: Oliver Wendell Holmes, the wit and writer, so a Holmes pun

explanation.surface: A clever joke by Oliver Wendell Holmes turns out to be plain stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. was a 19th-century American writer famed for his wit; 'Sounds like' says HOLMES PUN, spoken, gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Homespun cloth is woven at home, and figuratively the word means plain and unpretentious.

clue.text: Women may wear such, like the Boston Strangler.

definitions.meaning: second meaning: someone who chokes, as the notorious killer did

explanation.walkthrough: The Boston Strangler was a 1960s killer of women in Massachusetts.
explanation.definitionFit: A tight necklace worn round the throat and a person who throttles others share the name.

clue.text: The spoken form has a lot of noise–with a number being first or second, for instance.

definitions.text: a number being first or second, for instance

indicators.note: has means the spoken word holds the noise inside it

parts.note: oral means spoken
din is a loud noise

explanation.surface: Speech full of racket, with a figure being first or second.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordinal numbers such as first and second give position in a series rather than quantity.

clue.text: Most of what some write for the newspaper shows what the commuter may travel on. (But an early traveler was responsible for a place in five states!)

definitions.text: an early traveler was responsible for a place in five states
definitions.note: the explorer gave his name to a city found in several US states, such as Ohio and Georgia

indicators.note: most of means the final letter of the newspaper piece is dropped

parts.words: what some write for the newspaper
parts.note: a column is a regular newspaper article

parts.words: what the commuter may travel on
parts.note: a bus carries commuters

explanation.surface: A newspaper columnist explains how commuters get to work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of' drops the last letter of the newspaper feature, leaving COLUM. The definition sits in the bracket: the explorer whose name is borne by towns in five states.
explanation.definitionFit: Christopher Columbus, the explorer, is the namesake of cities including Ohio's capital.

clue.text: "Fab" owl in English shows–this might be a knotty problem!

definitions.text: this might be a knotty problem

indicators.note: shows means the answer is on display inside the run of clue words, spanning them

parts.note: the letters run from the end of Fab through owl and in to the start of English

explanation.surface: A splendid owl in English displays a tricky puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shows' signals that the answer is on view inside 'Fab owl in English', starting at the last letter of Fab.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowline is a sailor's knot, so it is literally a knotty matter.

clue.text: Makes an assertion in our country, being united.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ..., as a verb, declares
second meaning: the setter's country is the United ...

explanation.walkthrough: The Nation is an American magazine, so 'our country' is the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: To declare something is to state it, and America's divisions are its fifty member polities.

clue.text: Goes around and around–possibly someone like Nelson.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a swirl of water that goes round in circles, the verb used loosely for the noun
second meaning: Nelson ..., the American singer of film operettas

explanation.walkthrough: Nelson here is not the admiral but Nelson Eddy, singer and film star of the 1930s.
explanation.definitionFit: Whirling water is a swirl or whirlpool, and the singer's surname is the same word.

clue.text: See 11
See 11
What they work on might be safe, with the next-to last letter having things hatched this way.

definitions.text: What they work on might be safe
definitions.note: plural noun: the people who work on a safe

parts.note: Y is the next-to-last letter of the alphabet
eggs are hatched

explanation.surface: Criminals' target might be secure, with birds emerging from shells.
explanation.walkthrough: Yegg is old American slang for a burglar who cracks safes.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeggs are safecrackers, whose work is breaking into strongboxes.

clue.text: See 6
Study the writing–and don't take it out of this!

definitions.text: don't take it out of this

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart
text is a piece of writing

explanation.surface: Study the passage closely, and don't quote it selectively.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'taken out of context' means quoted without the surrounding words that fix its meaning.

clue.text: See 13
Known expressly? (One might be found in Somerset and the other in North Dakota.)

parts.words: One might be found in Somerset
parts.note: Wells is a cathedral city in Somerset, an English county
Fargo is the largest city in North Dakota

explanation.surface: A firm famous for express delivery, named after two distant towns.
explanation.walkthrough: Wells is a small cathedral city in the English county of Somerset.
explanation.definitionFit: Wells Fargo was famous as an express company, running stagecoach mail and freight.

clue.text: It's dumb, but it doesn't mean you can't see and feel and smell this way.

parts.words: but it doesn't mean you can't see and feel and smell this way
parts.note: the word looks as if it means lacking sight, touch and smell, yet in use it means foolish

explanation.surface: Something stupid that oddly doesn't mean you have lost your faculties.
explanation.definitionFit: Senseless means stupid or pointless, though literally it would mean lacking the five faculties.
